name: GI Joe fallacy
statement: Knowing that a bias exists is not enough to stop committing it, and the belief that knowing is enough is itself the mistake.
meaning: The name comes from the 1980s cartoon G. I. Joe, which closed each episode with 'Now you know. And knowing is half the battle.' Laurie Santos and Tamar Gendler took that line as the idea cognitive science should retire. Their claim has two parts. The first is that conscious knowledge of a situation is rarely what controls behaviour in it. The second is that people believe otherwise, and that belief is the fallacy proper. The essay presses the point on itself: knowing that the G. I. Joe fallacy is a fallacy is also less than half the battle. Ariella Kristal and Laurie Santos later split the cases in two. Encapsulated biases are ones where knowledge cannot reach the representation or the emotion driving the error, and they list visual illusions, implicit bias, the halo effect, hot and cold states, present bias and loss aversion. Attentional biases are ones knowledge could in principle fix, where people fail to attend to the right thing at the moment of choice, and they list anchoring, hindsight bias, confirmation bias, base-rate neglect, the planning fallacy, status quo bias, affective forecasting and intention attribution.

origin.who: Laurie R. Santos and Tamar Gendler
origin.where: Edge.org, in the annual question 'What scientific idea is ready for retirement?'
origin.note: A short essay under the title 'Knowing is Half the Battle'. It reports no data and names no studies, and its four illustrations are given without citations: the price 19.99 dollars against 20 dollars, a parole decision after a snack, a resume read with implicit bias, and fudge shaped like dog faeces.

evidence: The coinage carries no experiment of its own. The one sustained treatment is a Harvard Business School working paper by Kristal and Santos, number 21-084, which reviews existing findings and reports no new data. It opens with Daniel Kahneman on his own book: 'It's not a case of: Read this book and you'll think differently. I've written this book, and I don't think differently.' Its strongest single case is the halo effect, where Wetzel, Wilson and Kort tried forewarning and teaching participants about the effect. That paper is titled 'The halo effect revisited: Forewarned is not forearmed', and this entry takes its outcome from Kristal and Santos rather than from the paper, which was not obtained. Outside the review, the claim has been tested most directly on nudges, by telling people what a nudge is doing while it does it. Loewenstein, Bryce, Hagmann and Rajpal told people about the default options in a hypothetical advance medical directive, either before or after they filled it in, then let them revise. Their abstract records that the effect of the defaults persisted despite the disclosure, and that its effectiveness may therefore not depend on deceit. Bruns, Fillon, Maniadis and Paunov later pooled 23 publications built to compare transparent nudges against covert ones, holding 117 effect sizes. They report a positive effect of transparency on behavioural outcomes and no effect on non-behavioural ones. Default nudges supply 88% of those effects, and all but two of the studies ran online or in a laboratory.

replication.headline: No study testing the general claim was located. Its authors set that test as future work, and say that for some of the biases they cover they have only an anecdotal sense that knowing does not help.
replication.detail: There is no original result here to repeat. The 2014 essay is a coinage, and the 2021 review that defends it is a review. Kristal and Santos state the gap themselves: for some biases there is clear evidence that knowledge does not improve performance, and for others they have only an anecdotal sense, so future work should train subjects about a given bias and then test whether performance improves. Their two-category scheme is offered as a testable framework rather than a tested one, and no test of it was located. The narrower question, whether telling people about a mechanism blunts it, has been answered in one place. Disclosure did not remove the pull of a default in the advance-directive study, and in the pooled comparison of transparent against covert nudges the behavioural effect ran the other way, with transparency helping rather than hurting. The pooled estimate behind that direction sits behind a paywall and was not obtained, so only the direction and the study counts are reported here. The same review concedes ground on the other side. Attentional biases are described as cognitively penetrable, and Kristal and Santos cite work in which directing attention reduces the error, including football fans forecasting their mood more accurately after being asked how they would spend the day after the game.

limits: The claim is a slogan about a heterogeneous set of findings, which makes it hard to falsify as stated. Kristal and Santos restrict their review to prominent biases where some evidence about the role of knowledge already existed, and say other biases would need reviewing before the framework could be said to cover them. Their working paper appears to have stayed a working paper. A Crossref bibliographic search on its title and authors returned no journal version, and web search returned only the Harvard Business School copy. The nudge-transparency evidence is narrow in a way its own authors flag: default nudges dominate it, the settings are online or laboratory, and the outcome measured is whether a nudge still works, not whether a person's judgement improved. Searching for a direct test covered Crossref bibliographic queries, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC and general web search, pairing the term with experiment, replication, test and evidence. What came back was the term applied rather than examined. The related literature that does carry numbers is training, not telling, and this corpus keeps it under debiasing.
misreadings: The commonest error is to cite the GI Joe fallacy as a finding. It is a name for a pattern, published in an essay for a general audience, and a page that supports a claim by naming it has argued in a circle. A second error is to run it together with the bias blind spot, which is a measured asymmetry in how people rate themselves against others. The two point in opposite directions. The blind spot says people underestimate their own bias, while this says the people who do not underestimate it are no better off. Third, the coining essay's own illustrations have not all held. It asks the reader to picture a prisoner seeming a better candidate for parole after lunch, and grounds the picture in ego depletion. A registered replication across 23 laboratories and 2,141 people put the ego-depletion effect at d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15]. Fourth, 'knowing is not half the battle' is not 'nothing works'. Kristal and Santos expect attentional biases to respond to practice and to prompts, and single out Morewedge's training games as promising for that class while doubting they will touch encapsulated biases. The pooled evidence on teaching people about biases is in the debiasing entry, and it is smaller than the best-known single studies rather than absent.

sources.text: Santos, L. R., & Gendler, T. S. (2014). Knowing is half the battle. Edge.org, annual question: What scientific idea is ready for retirement? The essay that coins the term. Read in full.

Kristal, A. S., & Santos, L. R. (2021). G.I. Joe phenomena: Understanding the limits of metacognitive awareness on debiasing. Harvard Business School Working Paper 21-084. A review with no new data. No peer-reviewed version was located in Crossref or by web search.

Wetzel, C. G., Wilson, T. D., & Kort, J. (1981). The halo effect revisited: Forewarned is not forearmed. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 17(4), 427-439. The paper was not obtained; its title and bibliographic details were verified at Crossref, and what it found is reported here from Kristal and Santos.

Loewenstein, G., Bryce, C., Hagmann, D., & Rajpal, S. (2015). Warning: You are about to be nudged. Behavioral Science & Policy, 1(1), 35-42. The article is paywalled at Sage; the wording quoted here is from its abstract as served by the Semantic Scholar API.

Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics, 116, 102350. ScienceDirect returned 403; the abstract was read at the RePEc record and at the European Commission Joint Research Centre repository, which agree.
